cards.title: The revenue zigzag
cards.author: editorial
cards.why: It explains the critical fiscal relationship between the federation and provinces, providing insights into constitutional provisions and current economic challenges.
cards.summary: The federal government has reached an agreement with provinces to secure Rs1.035 trillion in cash grants to help meet its revenue targets. This deal, based on Article 164 of the Constitution, involves provinces returning a portion of their share from the 7th NFC Award. The arrangement is seen as a move by Islamabad to address its fiscal distress, though it raises questions about the long-term stability of current constitutional fiscal arrangements.
key_facts: The 7th NFC Award mandates that 57.5% of net federal taxes are transferred to the provinces.
Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa has agreed to contribute Rs157 billion annually to the federal exchequer.
Article 164 of the Constitution permits the federal government to grant funds to provinces or vice versa.
The former provincial government of K-P claimed Rs964 billion from the Federal Consolidated Fund.
The federal government is reportedly considering amendments to Article 160(3A) to alter revenue-sharing mechanisms.

vocab.meaning: Generous distribution of money or gifts.
The national treasury or public funds.
Threats or pressure used to force someone to do something.

text: A familiar jugglery of figures is underway between the federation and the provinces. Struggling to meet its revenue targets - and burdened by the 7th NFC Award, which hands 57.5% of net federal taxes to the provinces - Islamabad has struck a deal of convenience with the federating units. While the rationale behind this provincial largesse remains unclear, a staggering Rs1.035 trillion in cash grants will flow back to the federal exchequer. Even Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, long at odds with the Centre over its withheld dues, has agreed to pitch in Rs157 billion annually. This figure also absorbs the Rs17.8 billion previously deducted at source from the reluctant province's NFC share. The agreement signed earlier this month is being seen as a win-win proposition under Article 164 of the Constitution, which enables cash grants to the Centre. The point, however, is that it is a zigzag under duress, as the present political setup lacks credibility. K-P, under Governor's Rule, is obviously not in a position to put up any resistance, unlike the suspended two-thirds majority government of the PTI. Chief Minister Sohail Afridi had moved the Federal Constitutional Court claiming Rs964 billion from the Federal Consolidated Fund regarding the continued extension of the 7th NFC Award and the merger of the erstwhile FATA into the province. The additional funds sought by K-P were to the tune of over Rs1.6 trillion. The accord can only be seen as a respite for a cash-starved Islamabad. It is also an open secret that the federation hopes to claw back a bigger slice of revenue from the provinces - a move that would require amending the constitutional protection under Article 160(3A). The Centre says it needs money for expenditures on security and development projects. Rather than opting for credible austerity and belt-tightening to curb widespread leakages, the decision to bank on the provinces is an ill-advised initiative that contravenes the provincial autonomy exercised under the 18th Amendment. All that is needed is a new, non-partisan revenue distribution formula based on the provinces' human development indicators and revenue-generation capability.

cards.title: Wheat shortage
cards.author: editorial
cards.why: It highlights systemic failures in agricultural policy and food security management, which are frequent themes in exam questions.
cards.summary: Pakistan is facing a significant wheat shortage despite increased domestic production in the last fiscal year. Poor supply chain management, lack of effective forecasting, and market hoarding have caused retail flour prices to spike. Experts warn that the country remains heavily dependent on costly imports, putting further pressure on limited foreign exchange reserves.
key_facts: Pakistan produced 29.61 million tonnes of wheat in FY26, a 4.3% increase from the previous year.
The annual national consumption of wheat is estimated between 31 and 32 million tonnes.
Market estimates suggest a supply shortfall of three to four million tonnes before the next harvest.
Over 100,000 tonnes of wheat have been imported since late October.
Flour prices in some markets have reached Rs200 per kg.

vocab.meaning: Likely to change suddenly and unexpectedly, especially for the worse.
The action of obtaining or purchasing supplies.
To make two different ideas or facts consistent with each other.

text: Rising wheat and flour prices have placed another burden on Pakistani households, exposing serious shortcomings in the country's management of its most essential food commodity. Despite the arrival of more than 100,000 tonnes of imported wheat since late October, flour prices continue to climb, with some varieties now selling for as much as Rs200 per kg. Market estimates suggest a shortfall of three to four million tonnes before the next harvest, which in turn raises serious questions about the government's ability to anticipate demand and maintain adequate supplies. Pakistan's recurring wheat shortages cannot be attributed to inadequate production alone. The country harvested 29.61 million tonnes in FY26, an increase of 4.3% over the previous year, yet production remains insufficient to meet annual consumption of 31 to 32 million tonnes. With population growth steadily increasing demand, the absence of reliable forecasting, effective stock management and timely import decisions has compounded the problem. Warnings of an impending shortage were reportedly issued as early as May, but the authorities failed to respond with the urgency required. Equally concerning is the apparent disconnect between official assurances of sufficient wheat stocks and the realities of the market. Suspected hoarding and disruptions in interprovincial supplies have contributed to price volatility, while the benefits of imported wheat have yet to reach consumers. Dependence on imports to bridge domestic shortages also places an unnecessary strain on foreign exchange reserves. Federal and provincial authorities must therefore urgently reconcile production and consumption to ensure transparent distribution until the next harvest. Stronger market oversight and coordinated procurement arrangements are equally necessary. Ensuring an affordable and uninterrupted wheat supply - that too at reasonable prices - must remain a central priority of the country's agricultural and economic policies.

cards.title: India's bigoted voter purge
cards.author: editorial
cards.why: It provides a critical perspective on democratic erosion and minority rights in South Asia, relevant to International Relations and political science studies.
cards.summary: A massive deletion of 130 million names from Indian electoral rolls is raising alarms about the disenfranchisement of religious minorities. Critics argue these purges are targeted efforts to weaken opposition bases, particularly among Muslims and Dalits. The process has been linked to broader state agendas involving citizenship documentation and potential deportations.
key_facts: Approximately 130 million names have been removed from India's electoral rolls.
In West Bengal, Muslims made up 70% of the 2.7 million deleted names despite being 27% of the state's population.
Home Minister Amit Shah has linked voter roll revisions to issues of denaturalisation and deportation.
The BJP reportedly won elections in West Bengal for the first time after the deletion of nine million voters from the rolls.

vocab.meaning: To deprive someone of the right to vote.
To remove people or things from an organization in a sudden or violent way.
The act of taking away citizenship from a naturalized citizen.

text: The government of Prime Minister Narendra Modi continues to find new ways to insult the intelligence of its citizens and assault the rights of the country's minorities. The deletion of 130 million names from India's electoral rolls - the largest such purge in the nation's history - has nothing to do with electoral integrity, but rather is a bald-faced effort to disenfranchise Muslims and others who are unlikely to support the ruling BJP. In West Bengal, for example, Muslims constituted approximately 70% of the 2.7 million names deleted after closer review, despite making up only 27% of the population. Nationwide, rights groups have documented that the omissions fall disproportionately on religious minorities, Dalits and other marginalised communities. The consequences of removal from the rolls do not end with just disenfranchisement. In many cases, victims of the BJP's rigging exercise have wound up being detained, deported and stripped of citizenship. There have been cases of people being deported to countries they had never been to before. Home Minister Amit Shah - Modi's closest adviser - said out the quiet part loud at a recent rally in Haryana, explicitly linking voter roll revision to denaturalisation and deportation. If Shah's words reflect the actual thinking of the Indian government, the voter roll purges are not just a human rights violation, but could even meet the criteria for ethnic cleansing. It is also worth noting that the purges have already borne fruit. After deleting nine million voters, the BJP won elections in West Bengal for the first time ever. People protesting against the voter purge were beaten and jailed. Meanwhile, the prime minister has failed even to try to properly defend either the policy or its enforcement. But just as he has failed to hold a single actual press conference in almost 12 years as prime minister, Modi is getting what he wanted without having to answer to anyone, as India continues to move toward being a democracy for only the right kinds of people.

cards.title: Is China Misreading the Moment?
cards.author: Rush Doshi
cards.why: It touches on the shifting dynamics of US-China relations, a staple topic for international relations papers.
cards.summary: From the published summary: US President Donald Trump is scheduled to meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping during the APEC summit in Shenzhen. This meeting takes place against the backdrop of a temporary pause in the trade war that defined 2025.
key_facts: US President Donald Trump is attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen.
The meeting with Xi Jinping marks their fourth discussion as part of a recent diplomatic thaw.
The trade war of 2025 between the US and China is currently in a state of abeyance.

vocab.meaning: The easing of hostility or strained relations between countries.
A state of temporary disuse or suspension.
